[[Category:Normalisation Function]]
[[Category:Machine learning]]
[[File:Vector softmax.png|thumbnail|400px|Application of '''softmax''' on a column vector.]]
'''Softmax''' is a [[normalisation function]] that maps a [[vector]] of real-valued logits to a [[categorical probability distribution]].

== Definition ==

For $\vec z=(z_1,\dots,z_K)^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{K}$,

$$
\operatorname{softmax}(\vec z)_i
=
\frac{\exp(z_i)}
{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\exp(z_j)},
\qquad i=1,\dots,K.
$$

== Shift and numerical stability ==

In practice, it is evaluated with a shift for [[numerical stability]]. Let $m=\max_{j=1,\dots,K}z_j$; then

$$
\operatorname{softmax}(\vec z)_i
=
\frac{\exp(z_i-m)}
{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\exp(z_j-m)}.
$$

<blockquote>
Mathematically, the shift $m$ represents dividing both the numerator and denominator by $e^m$ to simplify calculation. e.g., to calculate the softmax of $\vec z = (100,102,101)^\top$, one calculate instead softmax of $\vec z - \vec 1 \cdot m = (100-m,102-m,101-m)^\top$, where $m$ can be, for example, $102$.
</blockquote>

== Temperature parameter ==
[[File:LLM temperature.png|thumbnail|400px|left|In a '''[[large language model (LLM)]]''', a higher temperature encourages the model to experiment more with less conventional sentence and passage structures, whereas a lower temperature encourages conservative, conventional construction.]]
A temperature parameter $\tau>0$ controls the sharpness of the distribution:

$$
\operatorname{softmax}(\vec z/\tau)_i
=
\frac{\exp(z_i/\tau)}
{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\exp(z_j/\tau)}.
$$

As $\tau\to 0^{+}$, the distribution approaches an [[one-hot vector]]; as $\tau\to\infty$, it approaches the [[uniform distribution]].

== Common form ==

Including both the shift and the temperature parameter:

$$
\operatorname{softmax}(\vec z/\tau)_i
=
\frac{\exp((z_i-m)/\tau)}
{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\exp((z_j-m)/\tau)}.
$$
where $m=\max_{j=1,\dots,K}z_j$ and $\tau \in (0,\infty)$.

== Properties ==

=== $\sum_{i=1,\dots,K} \operatorname{softmax}(\vec z/\tau)_i=1$ ===

as required to constitute a [[categorical probability distribution]].
